ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns, though formal presentation segments are long, slide-driven monologues. Early conversation is loose and social, with frequent greetings, acknowledgments, brief side exchanges, and occasional overlapping or interrupted starts; speakers often repeat words, restart phrases, and use fillers such as “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” and “you know.” The moderation becomes more structured for introductions, transitions, and Q&A, but remains warm and informal. Participants generally build on talks through praise followed by exploratory questions, often framing challenges softly—“I’m curious,” “do you think,” “have you looked at”—rather than directly disputing claims. Answers are thoughtful and hedged, using qualifiers like “I think,” “sort of,” “likely,” “we haven’t looked at that,” and “it’s early,” with speakers openly noting uncertainty and limits. Questions tend to be multipart, conversational, and sometimes reformulated midstream, while responses often begin by validating the question before narrowing or qualifying the answer.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Redesigning catch limits for a community-managed reef fishery so stocks recover without pushing families out of fishing.

speakers.name: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
speakers.background: A reef-fish population ecologist with 12 years of experience designing monitoring systems for community-managed coastal fisheries in the Pacific. She has led underwater visual censuses, benthic-habitat assessments, larval-recruitment monitoring, and spawning-aggregation counts, and routinely fits surplus-production and length-structured stock indicators to imperfect catch data. She coordinated the 2023-2025 reef-condition and aggregation surveys for this fishery.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames catch limits as a precautionary control on fishing mortality relative to reef productivity, recruitment variability, and the vulnerability of spawning aggregations. She sees the 2019-2025 cooperative records as the strongest initial quantitative anchor because they provide a repeated, species-specific time series from which trends, seasonal concentration, and potential depletion signals can be estimated. She is wary of treating one-time household reports as equivalent to longitudinal catch monitoring, while recognizing that missing removals must eventually be characterized.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Mateo R. de la Cruz
speakers.background: A fisheries and development economist with 9 years of experience analyzing small-scale fishery markets, cooperative transaction records, and household income risk. His applied work combines price-and-volume series, revenue decomposition, basic scenario modeling, and distributional analysis of management changes. He has previously helped local governments translate uncertain data into provisional harvest rules with explicit review points.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats the immediate problem as one of managing biological recovery while limiting abrupt income shocks for fishing households. He values the cooperative records because they link species landed, volume, prices, and registered owner revenue over several years, allowing an initial estimate of how alternative limits may affect earnings and volatility. He is cautious about inferring monetary losses from non-market harvest without clearer measurement, but supports using household evidence to test who is excluded from the transaction data and what a limit would mean beyond sales revenue.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Mereana Katoa
speakers.background: A maritime anthropologist with 15 years of field-based research on customary tenure, household labor, food sharing, and gendered work in coastal fishing communities. She designed the 2024 household livelihood survey and has conducted participant observation, semi-structured interviews, kinship mapping, and seasonal activity calendars with fishers, gleaners, processors, and households dependent on shared catch. As principal investigator, she is responsible for ensuring that the research process is credible to both the council and community members.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Understands fishing as a household and social-relations system rather than only a stream of market landings. She focuses on unpaid kin crew, shore-based gleaning, reciprocal distribution, and subsistence fish as forms of labor, nutrition, and obligation that may be invisible in buyer records. She can accept a time-sensitive provisional quantitative baseline when it is transparently bounded, but insists that excluded activities be documented and that the team establish a clear evidence-based point for revisiting the baseline before final limits are adopted.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

meeting_opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a dataset, one member objects once with a reason, and then stays silent about that decision. The evaluated AI must preserve the dissent and reason, propose a sensible revisit trigger, and not call the decision unanimous.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a dataset, one member objects once with a reason, and then stays silent about that decision. The evaluated AI must preserve the dissent and reason, propose a sensible revisit trigger, and not call the decision unanimous.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: In the meeting, the ecology lead recommends using the 2019-2025 buyers' cooperative landing records as the primary dataset for the initial catch-limit baseline because they provide the only multi-year species-specific catch series. The economics lead agrees, noting that the same records allow comparison of landed volume, prices, and registered fishers' revenue variation. The anthropology lead objects once: the records count registered boat owners but omit unpaid kin crew, shore-based gleaners, and fish distributed through customary sharing, so using them as the primary baseline may make the social burden of lower limits look smaller than it is. The project chair decides to use the cooperative landing records as the primary baseline so work can be completed for the 15 June council meeting. The chair assigns ecology and economics to prepare the baseline and assigns anthropology to document the omitted fishing and sharing activities using the 2024 household survey and short follow-up interviews. After stating the objection, the anthropology lead does not speak again about the dataset decision. No one claims the choice is unanimous. The meeting should leave a concrete revisit condition: the team will revisit whether the cooperative records remain the primary baseline if the anthropology follow-up shows that omitted fishing or sharing supplies at least 20% of household fish income or food fish among affected households, or if it identifies a group materially affected by the proposed limit that is absent from cooperative records. The follow-up evidence is due by 1 September, before final catch limits are adopted.

ground_truth.decision: The team selected the 2019-2025 buyers' cooperative landing records as the primary quantitative dataset for the initial catch-limit baseline, with reef surveys, spawning-aggregation counts, and household evidence used as supporting and follow-up evidence.

dissent.position: Objected to relying on the cooperative records as the primary baseline.
dissent.reason: The records cover registered boat owners and recorded sales but omit unpaid kin crew, shore-based gleaners, and customary sharing. This could understate who bears the livelihood and food-security effects of reduced catch limits.

ground_truth.agreement_status: The decision was made by the chair despite the anthropology objection; it was not unanimous.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: Good morning. Before we get into the updates, did anyone hear from Mateo? He said he might be coming straight from the cooperative office. For today, I think we need to leave with a defensible choice of primary quantitative baseline for the June proposal. Not necessarily a final quota number. I want us to be clear about what each dataset can actually support.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: Sorry, I was at the cooperative office. I missed the last meeting, so could I get the short version of where we landed on the baseline question? I've started tabulating the 2019 to 2025 records, and they're probably the strongest quantitative- sorry, the strongest anchor we have for the numbers, but only for marketed landings and registered owners, not total household fishing income.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: That’s essentially where we were. I’d recommend using the 2019–2025 cooperative series as the primary baseline, explicitly as a marketed-landings baseline, because it’s repeated and species-resolved. The reef and household material would then constrain how we interpret it, rather than us pretending they’re equivalent sampling frames. Mateo, from what you’ve tabulated so far, do price and owner-revenue patterns vary enough by season that an annual cap could concentrate hardship in particular months?

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: I haven't separated the series by month yet, so I wouldn't want to infer that from the annual tabulation. What concerns me is 2024. Volume fell in several high-value species, but recorded owner revenue stayed fairly steady because average price rose. Before we call that resilience, I need to check whether it's quality, timing, or just a different mix of boats selling through the cooperative. And Lani, do the spawning indicators suggest there are particular months we should treat separately?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: The aggregation signal points to a vulnerable seasonal window, but I would not specify months yet. The 2024 and 2025 counts need a comparability check on tidal window and observer coverage first. One heavily landed species was lower at the aggregation in 2025, sorry, in the 2025 count, without the same decline on adjacent transects, so that could be timing rather than depletion. Once that's checked, we can test whether the monthly landing and price series overlaps the aggregation period.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: That comparability check matters. From the household side, I'm comfortable treating the cooperative series as a provisional marketed-landings baseline, but not as a measure of household exposure. It leaves out kin crew, gleaners, and fish moved through sharing. Mateo, when owner revenue is standing in for economic exposure, what are we assuming about how catch, cash, and risk are actually distributed within a boat household?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: Mm, that is the concern.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: That is a real limitation. If we use owner revenue, we're assuming, at least provisionally, that the owner's recorded sales are a reasonable proxy for the household's exposure. But it doesn't tell us anything reliable about crew shares, unpaid labor, consumption from catch, or whether the owner absorbs a bad season rather than passing it on. Mereana, in the 2024 survey, which of those forms of dependence was, um, least visible in the cash-income questions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: The least visible was fish received and redistributed outside a sale. Cash questions captured some crew income, unevenly, but households often described food fish as an obligation or a reciprocal claim, rather than income, so they didn't necessarily report it that way. I need to check the instrument and the coding before saying how consistently we can compare that across households.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: That distinction is why I'd keep the 2019–2025 cooperative records labeled as marketed removals. I wouldn't inflate them into household catch. Mereana, when you check the coding, can you tell us whether received fish is separable from directly caught fish consistently enough to set a review threshold, say a level of unrecorded dependence where the initial baseline needs revisiting, or...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: I think that is workable, provided it is a real review condition and not just a footnote. I would use 1 September for the follow-up evidence, and revisit the baseline if omitted fishing or sharing accounts for at least 20% of food fish or fish income among affected households, or if we identify a materially affected group that's absent from the cooperative records. I need to verify first that the coding can support that comparison.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: I support making that a genuine review condition. For the 15 June proposal, I'd keep the baseline strictly to recorded marketed landings and show the distribution across registered owners. Then the 1 September check can tell us whether that limit is missing a group whose food or income exposure is substantial.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: That gives us a defensible sequence. The 2019–2025 cooperative records stay as the primary quantitative baseline for the June advice, and they're explicitly for recorded marketed landings. Then the 1 September household review is a condition on whether that framing is adequate. I would just avoid calling the limit protective of total removals until we know how large those omitted pathways are.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: Right, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: And for the June wording, I want to keep that distinction really clear. This is a provisional marketed-landings baseline, not an estimate of total removals or household burden. I’ll check whether the survey coding lets us apply the 20 percent condition consistently, rather than, um, treating the threshold as more precise than the data allow.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: Until that coding check is complete, I would not attach ecological meaning to the 20 percent figure either. The 2019–2025 cooperative records can still give us the species-specific trajectory and seasonal concentration we need for June, but the proposal should say plainly that it is controlling recorded marketed fishing mortality, not all reef- I mean, not all reef removals.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: Mm, yes.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: One practical point for the June analysis, I need to verify whether the 2019 and 2020 price fields are net of handling fees, and whether all buyers reported them in the same format. Until then, I'd present revenue changes cautiously, cautiously as recorded owner receipts, not necessarily directly comparable net earnings, and keep the proposed limit tied first to volumes by species.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: The biological screen should stay volume- and species-based at this stage. From the 2019–2025 cooperative landings, we can look at trajectories, concentration, and whether removals peak around the aggregation window, once I’ve checked the 2024–2025 count protocols. I wouldn’t let the revenue series- I wouldn’t let an uncertain revenue series determine the fishing-mortality control.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: Yes, that keeps the control aligned with what the records can actually show.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: Yes—the 2019–2025 cooperative series is the right anchor for that volume screen.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: I agree on the anchor, but let's keep that qualification visible in the June text. And when we describe household implications, I would avoid extrapolating from registered owners to households generally. The households reporting shortages despite high cooperative landings are exactly the pattern we need to understand before we make that claim.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: Yes—the 2019–2025 cooperative records should remain explicitly bounded that way.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. de la Cruz
transcript.text: All right, I think we can stop there and give everyone a few minutes back. Thank you, everyone. We'll pick this up once the checks are in.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lani Vaeasoani
transcript.text: Thank you, everyone. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mereana Katoa
transcript.text: Take care, everyone.
